texts.0: SP, due to mission planning conducted without the current publication for the route, did not plan the mission according to aircraft energy planning and did not prepare the alternate mission at all. Fuel figures, working area allocation and recovery times were left undefined and the mission planning sheets were still blank at step-in. IP had to rebuild the plan on the ground and dictate the fuel and area limits before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to a threat present in the minimum threat set but not identified during planning, did not take into consideration the forecast weather at the recovery time and left the alternate mission unplanned. The mission planning sheets were completed only after IP pointed out each missing entry in turn. The plan reached the lower limit of the standard solely through verbal prompting and delayed step-in by about ten minutes.
texts.2: SP, due to a currency shortfall that was not addressed at the start of the planning phase, first built an energy plan that did not cover the transit to the second working area. SP identified the discrepancy while reviewing the planning sheets and recomputed fuel, times and area allocation before the brief, without IP intervention. The completed plan covered the profile and the alternate mission with the required margin.
texts.3: SP planned the mission suitably according to aircraft energy planning and own training level, taking into consideration all data required for mission planning. Fuel, area allocation, timings and the alternate mission were computed correctly and the planning sheets were complete and legible at the briefing. No entry required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP produced a mission plan of exceptional quality, with energy planning, timings and the alternate mission computed to the minute and cross-checked against the Flight Manual and Local Area Procedures. Every contingency raised in the brief was already supported by figures SP had computed in advance. Deviations from the ideal plan were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP planned the mission within standards, but the energy plan was built on the minimum fuel figure with no usable reserve and the alternate mission was worked out in outline only. The trend is toward a plan that satisfies the requirement on paper while leaving nothing available for an unplanned delay or a runway change. SP is expected to compute realistic reserves and a fully developed alternate mission before the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP built a mission plan that met the code expected at this stage of training, with fuel and area allocation computed but the alternate mission left in outline only, due to the planning session being split with another ground duty ahead of the brief. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the alternate mission to the same level of detail as the primary plan on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP produced a complete energy plan including the alternate mission, due to a fuel figure on the second working area that had been carried over from an earlier profile and needed to be recalculated once noticed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check every inherited figure against the current profile before it is carried into a new plan.
texts_at.3: SP delivered a mission plan complete and legible at the brief, due to one area-allocation figure rounded from the planning table rather than copied from it directly, a difference of no operational consequence. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read every figure directly from the planning table so no rounding step remains in the process.

texts_above.2: SP planned the mission with fuel, area allocation and the alternate mission all computed and cross-checked ahead of the brief, one stage further than what is currently asked. Carrying the alternate mission to the same level of detail as the primary plan as a habit, rather than as an extra effort, would make the margin repeat itself without being asked. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good mission preparation.
texts_above.3: SP worked fuel, timings and the alternate mission to a level of detail normally expected later in training, with every figure checked against the Flight Manual before the brief. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good energy planning.
texts_above.4: SP produced a mission plan that needed no correction of any kind, with every contingency raised at the brief already supported by figures computed in advance. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent mission preparation.

error_modes.label: MISSION BRIEFING EXECUTION AND DECLARATION OF TRAINING HANDICAPS

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient preparation against the Mission Briefing Guide, did not execute the briefing in the prescribed order and omitted the maneuver sequence and the emergency review entirely. SP also did not inform IP of the handicaps carried over from the previous sorties. IP had to stop the briefing, take it over and rebrief the whole profile before the aircraft was accepted.
texts.1: SP, due to a briefing prepared from memory rather than from the Mission Briefing Guide, omitted the weather review and the abort criteria and stated own training handicaps only when asked directly. Each missing paragraph was covered only after IP prompted for it. The briefing ended at the lower limit of the standard and ran about fifteen minutes over the scheduled time.
texts.2: SP, due to an out-of-sequence start on the briefing guide, initially passed over the emergency review before the maneuver sequence. SP recognized the omission, returned to the emergency items and completed them in the correct order, and declared the outstanding training handicaps unprompted. The briefing was completed to standard without IP intervention and inside the scheduled time.
texts.3: SP executed the mission briefing according to the Mission Briefing Guide, covering every paragraph in sequence and in the time allotted. SP informed IP of the handicaps identified so far in training and tied them to specific objectives for the sortie. No item required prompting.
texts.4: SP executed an exceptional briefing, delivering every Mission Briefing Guide paragraph from a prepared flow and adding the specific handicaps carried over, with the corrective technique already proposed for each. The threat picture, abort criteria and alternate mission were presented so precisely that no clarification was required. Departures from the guide were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP executed the briefing within standards, but the emergency review and the abort criteria were delivered as a recitation with little reference to the actual conditions of the day. The trend is toward a briefing that covers the guide headings without converting them into decisions for this sortie. SP is expected to brief each contingency against the actual weather, runway and fuel state on the next event.

texts_at.1: SP delivered the mission briefing to the level expected at this stage, covering the maneuver sequence and the emergency review from the Mission Briefing Guide but stating the training handicaps only after being asked directly, due to the briefing having been rehearsed from memory rather than read paragraph by paragraph. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to state the training handicaps unprompted, as part of the guide sequence itself.
texts_at.2: SP executed the briefing in full guide order and inside the scheduled time, due to the emergency review being started slightly before the maneuver sequence and then resequenced once the order was noticed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to run the guide headings in their published order from the outset.
texts_at.3: SP briefed every paragraph of the Mission Briefing Guide in sequence and tied the training handicaps to the objectives of the sortie, due to one weather figure quoted from the forecast rather than the most recent update available at step-in. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to draw the last briefed figure from the most current source available.

texts_above.2: SP delivered the briefing from a prepared flow covering every Mission Briefing Guide paragraph and the specific handicaps carried from earlier training, with the corrective technique already proposed for two of them. Naming a corrective technique for every carried-over handicap, not only the two flagged, would extend the same standard across the whole briefing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound briefing preparation.
texts_above.3: SP presented the threat picture, abort criteria and alternate mission so precisely that no clarification was required from either seat, with the whole guide delivered inside the scheduled time. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed briefing technique.
texts_above.4: SP delivered a briefing that needed no clarification at any point, with the corrective technique for every declared handicap proposed in advance and the guide covered exactly to time. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional briefing execution.

texts.0: SP, due to running the cockpit checks from memory instead of reading the checklist, did not execute all checks according to check list and completed them in a non-standardized manner. More than five items were missed across the interior and before-start checks, including one affecting aircraft configuration. IP had to intervene, stop the sequence and direct a complete rerun of the checklist before start.
texts.1: SP, due to an accelerated pace adopted to make up lost time, did not execute the checks in an impeccable and standardized manner and left two or three items unread on the before-start and before-taxi checks. The omissions were recovered only after IP called for the missed items verbally. The checklist was completed at the limit of the acceptable standard and only after that prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption from an intercom call during the interior check, initially skipped one checklist item and read two others out of the published order. SP detected the break in the flow, returned to the last completed item and repeated the remainder in sequence without IP intervention. All checks were completed correctly with only a short delay.
texts.3: SP executed all checks according to check list, without IP intervention, in an impeccable and standardized manner. Every item was read, actioned and verified in the published order, with responses given in standard phraseology and at a steady pace. No item was missed or repeated out of sequence.
texts.4: SP executed the checks to an exceptional standard, running each phase as a disciplined read-and-verify with the switch confirmed by touch before the response was given. The pace was uniform, the phraseology standard throughout, and one incorrectly positioned switch was identified and corrected during the check itself. Omissions were nil.
texts.marginal: SP executed all checks within standards, but the responses on the before-taxi check were given a fraction ahead of the actual switch confirmation on several items. The trend is toward a checklist read as a familiar rhythm rather than as a challenge and verified response. SP is expected to confirm each switch position physically before answering on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP completed the before-start and before-taxi checks to the level expected at this stage, reading every item but giving two or three responses a step ahead of the matching switch check, due to a pace set to make up time lost earlier at the aircraft. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold the response until the switch position is actually confirmed.
texts_at.2: SP completed all checks correctly and in the published order, due to an intercom call during the interior check that broke the flow and required the last item to be repeated once the call ended. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete a call before returning to the checklist rather than continuing to read through it.
texts_at.3: SP ran every check in an impeccable and standardized manner, due to one response on the before-taxi check given a fraction ahead of the physical switch confirmation, corrected within the same item. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the switch by touch before the response is given on every item without exception.

texts_above.2: SP read, actioned and verified every checklist item in the published order and at a steady pace, recovering cleanly from one interruption by an intercom call without losing a single item. Repeating the last completed item rather than the one after the interruption, on every occasion, would remove any doubt about where the flow resumes. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid checklist discipline.
texts_above.3: SP ran each phase of the checklist as a disciplined read-and-verify with every switch confirmed by touch before the response was given, and one incorrectly positioned switch was found and corrected during the check itself. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed checklist technique.
texts_above.4: SP ran the checklist with uniform pace and standard phraseology throughout, catching a misplaced switch during the check itself with no item missed or repeated out of sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding checklist discipline.

error_modes.label: COMPLETENESS OF LAP AND SOP PROCEDURE SEQUENCE

texts.0: SP, due to an unwritten local practice followed in place of the published procedure, skipped procedures required by Local Area Procedures and SOPs, including the walk-around sequence and the pre-taxi radio setup. The aircraft was configured for taxi with the flight plan and frequencies unset. IP had to intervene, halt the aircraft and run the omitted procedures from the start.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on the previous sortie flow rather than on the applicable SOP, skipped two procedural steps of the ground sequence and performed the ejection seat and canopy checks out of the prescribed order. The steps were recovered only after repeated verbal reminders from IP. Procedural compliance ended at the lower limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an unfamiliar parking spot that changed the usual flow, initially omitted one SOP step in the pre-taxi sequence. SP recognized the gap before requesting taxi, stopped, completed the omitted step and resumed the sequence at the correct point without IP intervention. No procedure was left out and the delay was under one minute.
texts.3: SP did not skip any procedure according to Local Area Procedures and SOPs, executing the ground sequence complete and in the published order. Walk-around, strap-in, pre-start, start and pre-taxi flows were performed as written and at the correct trigger points. Nothing required prompting or repetition.
texts.4: SP executed the full Local Area Procedures and SOP ground sequence with exceptional discipline, adapting to a changed parking position and a delayed ground power connection without dropping or reordering a single step. SP additionally verified the applicable NOTAM and runway data at the point the SOP requires it. Procedural deviations were nil.
texts.marginal: SP completed the SOP ground sequence within standards, but several steps were performed noticeably later than their published trigger point and clustered together just before taxi. The trend is toward compressing the ground flow into the final minutes, which leaves no capacity for an unexpected item. SP is expected to run each procedure at its correct trigger point on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP completed the ground sequence to the level expected at this stage, running the walk-around, strap-in and pre-taxi flows in order but performing the ejection seat and canopy checks slightly out of sequence, due to reliance on the flow of the previous sortie rather than the applicable SOP for this aircraft change. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the applicable SOP for the specific procedure sequence before relying on a remembered flow.
texts_at.2: SP executed the full ground sequence in the published order, due to an unfamiliar parking spot that changed the usual flow and produced one omitted pre-taxi step before it was caught. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to run the SOP sequence from the published order rather than from the layout of the ramp.
texts_at.3: SP performed the ground sequence complete and in the published order, due to the applicable NOTAM being checked slightly later in the flow than the SOP trigger point, though before it was needed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move the NOTAM check to its published trigger point.

texts_above.2: SP ran the walk-around, strap-in, pre-start, start and pre-taxi flows complete and in the published order despite a changed parking position, recovering the one omitted step before it affected the sequence. Checking the NOTAM and runway data at the SOP trigger point on every sortie, not only when the layout changes, would remove the last variable from the flow. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady procedural compliance.
texts_above.3: SP adapted to a changed parking position and a delayed ground power connection without dropping or reordering a single SOP step, and additionally verified the applicable NOTAM and runway data at the correct trigger point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate procedural sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP ran the complete ground sequence through a changed parking position and a delayed ground power connection with no step dropped, reordered or repeated, checking the NOTAM and runway data exactly at the SOP trigger point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary procedural discipline.

error_modes.label: GROUND CREW COORDINATION AND CLEARANCE BEFORE SWITCH OR CONTROL ACTIVATION

texts.0: SP, due to failure to pass a required call at the briefed point, did not cooperate with the ground crew and left a clear misapprehension over the intended start sequence unresolved. SP moved the control surfaces and selected the fuel pump without being aware of the ground crew position and without acknowledging the marshaller. IP had to intervene, stop the action and re-establish contact with the crew before the start was continued.
texts.1: SP, due to an indirect hint instead of a direct statement of intent to the ground crew, allowed a misapprehension over the chocks and ground power sequence to persist. SP began the control check with the crewman still inside the wingtip arc and stopped only when IP called it verbally. Coordination was restored at the limit of the acceptable standard and only after that intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a hand signal given before eye contact was established, initially started the control sweep without positive acknowledgement from the marshaller. SP recognized the missing acknowledgement, stopped the control movement, obtained a clear thumbs-up and repeated the check with the crew visibly clear. The sequence was corrected in good time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP cooperated with the ground crew without allowing misapprehensions, using standard signals and confirming each one before acting. SP was aware of the ground crew position before activating any switch and before moving any aircraft control, verifying the area clear on both sides. The start, control check and chock removal were coordinated without hesitation.
texts.4: SP coordinated with the ground crew to an exceptional standard, briefing the start sequence to the marshaller in advance and confirming positive acknowledgement before every switch selection and control movement. When the crewman changed position during the start, SP paused the sequence and re-established visual contact before continuing. No ambiguity arose at any point.
texts.marginal: SP coordinated with the ground crew within standards, but on two occasions the switch selection followed the signal so closely that the crew acknowledgement had not yet been confirmed. The trend is toward assuming the expected response rather than observing it. SP is expected to hold each action until the ground crew acknowledgement is positively seen on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP coordinated with the ground crew to the level expected at this stage, using standard signals for the start and the chock removal but beginning the control sweep before the marshaller's acknowledgement had been positively seen on one occasion, due to a hand signal given before eye contact with the crew was established. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold each control movement until the acknowledgement is actually seen, not assumed from the timing of the signal.
texts_at.2: SP coordinated the start, control check and chock removal without allowing a misapprehension to develop, due to a control sweep begun before the marshaller's thumbs-up was confirmed and then corrected once the missing acknowledgement was noticed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to pause after every signal until the acknowledgement is seen, before any control is moved.
texts_at.3: SP confirmed the ground crew position before every switch and control movement, due to one hand signal given a beat before eye contact with the crew was fully established, though acted on only after acknowledgement followed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to establish eye contact first on every signal, as a fixed habit rather than as a recovered step.

texts_above.2: SP used standard signals and confirmed each one before acting for the start, the control check and the chock removal, recognizing and correcting one early control movement before the crew was clear. Verifying eye contact before the signal itself, rather than at the same moment, would remove the need for that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable ground crew coordination.
texts_above.3: SP briefed the start sequence to the marshaller in advance and confirmed positive acknowledgement before every switch selection and control movement, pausing to re-establish visual contact when the crewman changed position mid-sequence. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good coordination technique.
texts_above.4: SP coordinated every switch selection and control movement with a confirmed acknowledgement from the ground crew and resolved a mid-sequence position change without any ambiguity at any point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior ground crew coordination.

error_modes.label: AIRCRAFT CONDITION ASSESSMENT AND FLIGHT PERMISSIBILITY DECISION

texts.0: SP, due to a walk-around performed without reference to the Flight Manual limits, did not specify the aircraft condition correctly and could not decide its flight permissibility. SP overlooked an open write-up in the aircraft forms and a fluid trace on the left main gear, and declared the aircraft serviceable. IP had to intervene, re-inspect the aircraft and reverse the acceptance decision.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete knowledge of the limits applicable to the accepted deferred defects, could not state the aircraft condition confidently and hesitated over the flight permissibility decision. The correct assessment was reached only after IP directed SP to the relevant forms entry and the applicable limitation. The decision was made at the lower limit of the standard and only through that guidance.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial reading of the aircraft forms that missed one deferred item, first assessed the aircraft as fully serviceable. SP re-checked the forms before strap-in, identified the deferred item, verified its applicable limitation in the Flight Manual and restated the flight permissibility decision correctly without IP intervention. The correction was made before any further action was taken.
texts.3: SP specified the aircraft condition and decided its flight permissibility correctly and confidently. The walk-around, forms review and cockpit condition check were tied together into a clear serviceability statement, with each deferred item matched to its limitation. The decision was made without hesitation and required no confirmation from IP.
texts.4: SP assessed the aircraft condition to an exceptional standard, identifying a discrepancy not previously recorded, matching it against the Flight Manual limitations and stating the flight permissibility decision with the applicable reference quoted. The assessment was complete, confident and made without delay to the schedule. Nothing in the condition of the aircraft was left undefined.
texts.marginal: SP assessed the aircraft condition within standards, but the flight permissibility statement was made tentatively and only after a second look at the forms. The trend is toward an assessment that is technically correct yet delivered without the confidence the decision requires. SP is expected to state the serviceability decision clearly and on the first pass at the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP reached the aircraft condition and flight permissibility decision expected at this stage, tying the walk-around and the forms review into a serviceability statement but stating it tentatively and only after a second look at the forms, due to an initial reading of the deferred-item entry that was not immediately matched to its limitation. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to match every deferred item to its limitation on the first pass through the forms.
texts_at.2: SP restated the flight permissibility decision correctly after re-checking the aircraft forms, due to an initial reading that missed one deferred item before strap-in. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the forms review before the first serviceability statement is made, rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP specified the aircraft condition and decided its flight permissibility confidently, due to the applicable Flight Manual limitation being located a moment after the deferred item itself was identified, rather than in the same glance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read the limitation and the deferred entry together as one action.

texts_above.2: SP tied the walk-around, the forms review and the cockpit condition check into a clear serviceability statement, catching one missed deferred item on a self-initiated re-check before strap-in. Reading every deferred entry against its Flight Manual limitation on the first pass, rather than the second, would remove the need for that re-check. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured condition assessment.
texts_above.3: SP identified a discrepancy not previously recorded, matched it against the Flight Manual limitations and stated the flight permissibility decision with the reference quoted, without delay to the schedule. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise serviceability assessment.
texts_above.4: SP completed a serviceability assessment that left nothing about the aircraft condition undefined, identifying and referencing a discrepancy not previously recorded with no delay to the schedule. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate condition assessment.

error_modes.label: KNOWLEDGE AND HANDLING OF AIRCRAFT LEVERS AND SWITCHES

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient cockpit familiarization before the sortie, did not know or use correctly the aircraft levers and switches. SP selected the wrong panel on two occasions and moved a lever past the intended detent, producing a configuration that did not match the checklist step being run. IP had to intervene, restore the correct configuration and identify the controls for SP.
texts.1: SP, due to a cockpit flow learned by position rather than by function, hesitated over two switch selections and had to search the panel for a third. Correct selection was achieved only after IP identified the control verbally. Switch handling remained at the limit of the acceptable standard and slowed the ground sequence noticeably.
texts.2: SP, due to an inadvertent reach toward the adjacent switch during the after-start flow, initially placed a hand on the wrong selector. SP identified the error before the switch was moved, verified the correct control against the checklist and completed the selection properly without IP intervention. The remainder of the flow was run without further hesitation.
texts.3: SP knew and used correctly all aircraft levers and switches, selecting each control by function and confirming its position before moving on. Every selection was made at the correct point of the flow, with the correct grip and to the correct detent. No control was searched for and none was misidentified.
texts.4: SP handled the cockpit controls to an exceptional standard, selecting every lever and switch without visual search and confirming each position by touch and by indication. When a switch was found out of its normal position at strap-in, SP identified it immediately and restored the correct configuration. Handling errors were nil.
texts.marginal: SP used the aircraft levers and switches within standards, but two selections in the after-start flow required a brief visual search before the hand moved. The trend is toward controls located by memory of appearance rather than by an established flow. SP is expected to consolidate the cockpit flow so that each control is reached directly on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP operated the aircraft levers and switches to the level expected at this stage, selecting each control correctly but searching briefly for one panel before the after-start flow was complete, due to a cockpit flow still learned by position rather than by function. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to learn each control by its function so the search is no longer needed.
texts_at.2: SP completed the after-start flow with every control correctly selected, due to an inadvertent reach toward the adjacent switch that was caught and corrected before it was moved. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to verify the control against the checklist before the hand moves, not after it arrives.
texts_at.3: SP knew and used every aircraft lever and switch correctly, due to one selection confirmed by a brief glance rather than by touch alone before it was made. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm position by touch first, using the glance only to verify it afterward.

texts_above.2: SP selected every control by function and confirmed its position before moving on, catching one hand placed on the wrong selector before it was moved. Confirming position by touch on every selection, rather than after this one recognized near-miss, would remove the last visual check from the flow. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent switch handling.
texts_above.3: SP selected every lever and switch without visual search, confirming each position by touch and by indication, and restored one switch found out of position at strap-in immediately on noticing it. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined cockpit flow.
texts_above.4: SP handled every cockpit control without visual search and with no handling error across the whole flow, restoring one switch found out of position at strap-in the instant it was noticed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless switch handling.

error_modes.label: TAXI ROUTE COMPLIANCE AND CLEARANCE OF THE GROUND PATH

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect reading of the taxi clearance that was not verified against the airfield chart, did not follow the specified taxi route and did not ensure the ground path was clear of obstacles. SP turned onto the wrong taxiway and closed to within a wingspan of a parked aircraft without reducing speed. IP had to take control, stop the aircraft and taxi it clear.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the cockpit displays instead of outside the aircraft, drifted off the taxiway centerline by more than half the main gear track and approached the marked obstacle clearance line on the right. The correction was applied only after IP called for it, and the deviation reached the limit of the acceptable taxi corridor before it was stopped.
texts.2: SP, due to a late identification of the intersection while comparing the chart with the clearance, initially began the turn onto the wrong taxiway. SP recognized the error within a few meters, stopped the turn, confirmed the correct routing and regained the assigned taxiway centerline without IP intervention. Clearance from obstacles was maintained throughout.
texts.3: SP followed the specified taxi route and ensured that the ground path of the aircraft was clear of obstacles. The centerline was maintained within the main gear track throughout, turns were made at the correct intersections, and wingtip clearance from parked aircraft and equipment was continuously assessed. No correction was necessary.
texts.4: SP followed the assigned taxi route with exceptional precision, keeping the nose gear on the centerline through every turn and clearing the ground path visually well before each intersection. When ground equipment was found encroaching on the taxiway edge, SP identified it early, adjusted the path within the available surface and reported it on the ground frequency. Deviations were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP followed the specified taxi route within standards, but the aircraft rode consistently to the left of the centerline and the corrections were made in a series of late inputs at each turn. The trend is toward a track flown by reference to the nearest edge rather than to the centerline. SP is expected to establish and hold the centerline reference throughout the taxi on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP followed the taxi route and kept the ground path clear of obstacles to the level expected at this stage, holding the centerline reference for most of the route but riding slightly left of it, due to attention divided between the cockpit displays and the taxiway outside. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the centerline in view continuously rather than checking it between glances at the displays.
texts_at.2: SP regained the assigned taxiway centerline and maintained clearance from obstacles throughout, due to a late identification of the intersection while comparing the chart with the clearance that led to a turn started onto the wrong taxiway before it was corrected. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to identify the intersection from the chart before the turn point is reached, not while approaching it.
texts_at.3: SP followed the specified taxi route with wingtip clearance from parked aircraft continuously assessed, due to one turn taken a few feet wide of the ideal line while ground equipment was being cleared visually. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to clear the ground equipment and set the turn line as two separate checks rather than one combined glance.

texts_above.2: SP followed the specified taxi route with the centerline held inside the main gear track for the whole taxi, recognizing and correcting one early turn onto the wrong taxiway within a few meters. Confirming the intersection against the chart before reaching it, rather than while turning, would remove the correction altogether. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good taxi route discipline.
texts_above.3: SP kept the nose gear on the centerline through every turn and cleared the ground path visually well before each intersection, identifying encroaching ground equipment early and adjusting the path within the available surface. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good taxi technique.
texts_above.4: SP held the centerline through every turn of the taxi route with the ground path cleared well ahead of each intersection, adjusting once for encroaching ground equipment with no loss of track. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent taxi route discipline.

error_modes.label: TAXI SPEED CONTROL, STOPPING WITHOUT OSCILLATIONS AND HOLDING THE AIRCRAFT STATIONARY

texts.0: SP, due to power left set well above taxi requirements and braking applied only at the last moment, did not stop the aircraft as required and produced repeated pitching oscillations on the gear at every stop. SP also allowed the aircraft to creep forward during the leak check and again on the line-up, when it should have been halted. IP had to intervene on the brakes and stop the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a taxi speed carried above walking pace into the confined area, arrived at the holding point fast and stopped only with a hard brake application that set up two clear fore-and-aft oscillations. The aircraft came to rest a full aircraft length past the holding line and was held there only after IP called for brakes. Speed and stopping control remained at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction after the turn out of the parking area, initially allowed the taxi speed to build above that required for the ramp. SP recognized the excess, reduced power and used smooth braking to stop the aircraft on the holding line without oscillation and without IP intervention. The aircraft was then held stationary for the whole leak check.
texts.3: SP stopped the aircraft as required, without oscillations and without IP intervention, using a taxi speed appropriate to the area and to the surface conditions. Braking was smooth and progressive, each stop was made on the intended mark, and the aircraft was held completely stationary where the procedure required it. Power and brake use remained coordinated throughout.
texts.4: SP controlled taxi speed to an exceptional standard, anticipating each stop with an early power reduction so that only light braking was needed, and bringing the aircraft to rest precisely on the mark with no perceptible pitching. The aircraft was held rock steady through the leak check and the line-up with no creep at any time. Deviations from the intended stopping point were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP stopped the aircraft within standards, but each stop was achieved with a single firm brake application that produced a slight nose-down settle before the aircraft came to rest. The trend is toward speed managed by the brakes rather than by power planning ahead of the stop. SP is expected to reduce power earlier and stop with progressive braking on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP stopped the aircraft to the level expected at this stage without oscillation on the holding line, due to a taxi speed that briefly exceeded that appropriate to the confined parking row before it was reduced and the aircraft brought smoothly to rest. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power on entering a confined area before the speed has a chance to build.
texts_at.2: SP stopped the aircraft on the holding line without oscillation and without intervention, due to a delayed power reduction after the turn out of the parking area that allowed taxi speed to build above that required for the ramp before it was corrected. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reduce power as the turn is completed rather than after the straight taxi has resumed.
texts_at.3: SP stopped the aircraft as required, using a taxi speed appropriate to the area throughout, due to one stop made with a slightly firmer brake application than the surface required, though without any oscillation resulting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to ease the brake application further on a similar surface so power planning alone accounts for the stop.

texts_above.2: SP stopped the aircraft on the holding line using smooth, progressive braking with no oscillation, recognizing and correcting an excess taxi speed picked up after the turn out of the parking area before it affected the stop. Reducing power at the turn itself, rather than after the straight taxi resumed, would remove the correction from the sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound taxi speed control.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated every stop with an early power reduction so that only light braking was needed, bringing the aircraft to rest precisely on the mark with no perceptible pitching through the leak check and the line-up. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed speed and brake technique.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated every stop of the taxi sequence with power alone, needing only light braking to bring the aircraft to rest precisely on the mark with no perceptible pitching at any point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional taxi speed control.

error_modes.label: COORDINATION WITH IP ON THE (BOTH) PROCEDURES

texts.0: SP, due to reluctance to challenge a decision perceived as the instructor prerogative, did not ask the IP about the (BOTH) procedures and acted on an assumption of what had been intended. SP carried out the selection without any call to the front cockpit and without waiting for an answer, leaving the two cockpits with different understandings of the aircraft configuration. IP had to intervene, stop the action and restate the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to an unvoiced disagreement with the sequence because of the evaluation relationship, asked about the (BOTH) procedures in terms so tentative that no clear answer was returned, and then proceeded anyway. The coordination was established only after IP directed SP to make the call properly. The exchange met the requirement at its lower limit and only after that prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to deference to the front cockpit that initially replaced own assessment, started the (BOTH) selection before the reply from IP had been received. SP recognized the omission within a second or two, stopped the action, made the required call and waited for the answer before continuing, without IP intervention. Both cockpits then held the same picture of the configuration.
texts.3: SP asked the IP about the (BOTH) procedures and waited for the answer before acting, using clear and standard wording. The call was made at the correct point of the sequence and the action followed only once the reply had been received and understood. Both cockpits remained aligned on the aircraft configuration throughout.
texts.4: SP coordinated the (BOTH) procedures to an exceptional standard, stating the intended selection and the reason for it, waiting for the IP answer and reading back the direction received before acting. When the reply differed from the expectation, SP queried it directly and resolved the difference before any switch was moved. Coordination was complete at every step.
texts.marginal: SP asked about the (BOTH) procedures within standards, but the pause between the question and the action left barely enough time for a reply, and the acknowledgement was not read back. The trend is toward a call made to satisfy the requirement rather than to obtain an answer. SP is expected to wait for and confirm the IP response before acting on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP coordinated the (BOTH) procedures to the level expected at this stage, waiting for the IP reply before acting on most calls, due to one call made in terms tentative enough that the reply was less definite than the sequence needed before SP proceeded. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to phrase each call so that a clear answer is the only possible reply.
texts_at.2: SP completed the (BOTH) selection only after the IP reply had been received and understood, due to the action having been started before the reply arrived and then paused and restarted correctly once the omission was noticed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to wait for the reply before beginning the action, not while it is already under way.
texts_at.3: SP asked about the (BOTH) procedures and waited for the answer before acting, due to the pause between the question and the action leaving little more than the minimum time for a reply on one occasion. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to build a longer pause into the call so the timing no longer depends on how quickly the reply arrives.

texts_above.2: SP made the (BOTH) call at the correct point of the sequence and acted only once the reply had been received, recognizing and correcting one selection begun before the answer had actually arrived. Building in a longer pause after every call, not only after this recognized case, would remove the risk of acting early again. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid coordination discipline.
texts_above.3: SP stated the intended selection and the reason for it, waited for the IP answer and read back the direction received before acting, querying one reply that differed from the expectation before any switch was moved. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed crew coordination.
texts_above.4: SP stated the intended selection with its reason, read back the reply before acting and resolved one difference from the expected answer before any switch was moved, with coordination complete at every step. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding crew coordination.

error_modes.label: EXTERIOR INSPECTION WALK AROUND PATTERN AND LEAK DETECTION

texts.0: SP, due to a walk around started at the nose instead of behind the left wing and run against the clockwise direction, did not cover the wheel well, speed brake and engine bay areas and did not reference the checklist at any point. Flight gloves were not worn and the control surfaces were manhandled against their stops. IP stopped the inspection, repeated the walk around from the correct start point and found fluid along the fairing doors that SP had passed over.
texts.1: SP, due to a walk around executed from memory rather than from the checklist, skipped the leak check at the wheel well and the engine bay and had to be told to don flight gloves before touching the aircraft. Each omitted station was covered only after IP called it out in turn. The inspection reached the lower limit of the standard through verbal prompting alone and took about ten minutes longer than briefed.
texts.2: SP, due to breaking the clockwise sequence to answer the crew chief at the right main gear, initially left the speed brake bay and the left fairing seams unchecked. SP recognized the break, returned two stations upstream and completed the pattern, finding a fluid trace along a line coupling and reporting it to qualified maintenance personnel. The inspection was completed to standard without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the exterior inspection wearing flight gloves, beginning behind the left wing and moving about the aircraft in a clockwise direction in accordance with the checklist. Wheel well, speed brake and engine bay areas were examined for fluid leaks, fairing doors, seams and line couplings were checked, and no control surface was manhandled. Tire condition was assessed against the planned mission and the checklist was referenced to confirm every item complete.
texts.4: SP executed an exceptional exterior inspection, holding the clockwise pattern from behind the left wing and pausing at each leak prone area to check fairing doors, seams and line couplings in good light. SP identified a tire wear pattern that was marginal for the planned mission and raised it with qualified maintenance personnel before it appeared in the forms. Departures from the prescribed walk around were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed the exterior inspection within standards, but the pattern was executed quickly and the wheel well and engine bay areas received little more than a glance. The trend is toward a walk around that satisfies the sequence while relying on maintenance to have found everything first. SP is expected to slow the pattern at the leak prone areas and confirm each item against the checklist on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP executed the exterior inspection to the level expected at this stage, wearing flight gloves and following the clockwise pattern from behind the left wing, due to the sequence being broken once to answer the crew chief at the right main gear and resumed two stations upstream rather than at the exact point of the interruption. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to resume the pattern at the exact point of any interruption rather than a station or two before it.
texts_at.2: SP completed the exterior inspection to the checklist with a fluid trace found and reported to qualified maintenance personnel, due to the clockwise sequence being broken to answer the crew chief at the right main gear, leaving the speed brake bay and left fairing seams briefly unchecked before the pattern was resumed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the current station before responding to a call from the ground crew.
texts_at.3: SP examined the wheel well, speed brake and engine bay areas for fluid leaks and checked fairing doors, seams and line couplings in the published clockwise pattern, due to the tire condition assessment against the planned mission being made a station later than the walk-around trigger point, though before the inspection was called complete. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to assess tire condition at its own station rather than folding it into a later one.

texts_above.2: SP held the clockwise pattern from behind the left wing and recognized a break in the sequence caused by a crew chief call, returning two stations upstream to complete the pattern and finding a fluid trace along a line coupling that was reported to qualified maintenance personnel. Resuming exactly at the point of interruption, rather than a station or two before it, would tighten the pattern further without losing the find. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady inspection discipline.
texts_above.3: SP held the clockwise pattern from behind the left wing and paused at each leak-prone area in good light, identifying a tire wear pattern marginal for the planned mission and raising it with qualified maintenance personnel before it appeared in the forms. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate inspection technique.
texts_above.4: SP held the full clockwise pattern through an interruption from the crew chief and identified a tire wear pattern marginal for the mission before it reached the forms, referencing the checklist throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary exterior inspection technique.

error_modes.label: A/C FORMS CHECK BEFORE INITIATING ANY INSPECTION OR CHECKLIST

texts.0: SP, due to stepping to the aircraft without opening the AFTO Form 781, initiated the exterior inspection and the interior checklist before any form had been checked. An open write up affecting the planned mission was therefore never seen and SP declared the aircraft accepted. IP had to halt the strap in, return SP to the forms and contact maintenance for clarification before the sortie could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the forms as a formality to be cleared after the walk around, checked the AFTO Form 781 only after the exterior inspection had begun and did not query an entry that was incomplete. SP contacted maintenance only when IP pointed at the open item. The acceptance decision reached the lower limit of the standard and rested entirely on IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed first pass over the AFTO Form 781 while the refuelling crew was still at the aircraft, initially missed a servicing entry that had not been signed off. SP returned to the forms before starting the exterior inspection, identified the unsigned entry and contacted maintenance for clarification unprompted. The aircraft was accepted only after the form was accurate.
texts.3: SP checked the AFTO Form 781 before any aircraft inspection, other action or checklist was initiated, and read the open write ups against the requirements of the planned mission. A discrepancy in the form was reported to maintenance and resolved before acceptance. SP specified the aircraft condition and decided its flight permissibility correctly and confidently.
texts.4: SP reviewed the AFTO Form 781 in full before any other action, cross checking the open write ups and the servicing entries against the profile and the fuel plan for the sortie. One ambiguous entry was clarified with maintenance and annotated before the walk around began, so no question over acceptability of the aircraft remained at any point. Deviations from the prescribed sequence were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP checked the forms before starting the inspection and accepted the aircraft within standards, but the review was limited to the last page and the older open write ups were not read. The trend is toward an acceptance decision made on the assumption that anything significant would have been briefed. SP is expected to read the full AFTO Form 781 and resolve every question with maintenance before the next acceptance.

texts_at.1: SP checked the AFTO Form 781 before the exterior inspection to the level expected at this stage, due to a first pass made while the refuelling crew was still at the aircraft that missed one servicing entry before it was picked up on the return to the forms. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the forms review once the refuelling crew has cleared the aircraft rather than while they are still present.
texts_at.2: SP identified an unsigned servicing entry and contacted maintenance for clarification before accepting the aircraft, due to a rushed first pass over the form while the refuelling crew was still present that missed the entry before the forms were checked again ahead of the exterior inspection. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the first pass of the forms only once the aircraft area is clear of servicing activity.
texts_at.3: SP checked the AFTO Form 781 before any inspection or checklist and resolved a discrepancy with maintenance before acceptance, due to one servicing entry read a line out of order before being matched correctly to the open write-up it referred to. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read the form top to bottom in one pass so entries are not matched out of order.

texts_above.2: SP reviewed the AFTO Form 781 before the exterior inspection and caught one unsigned servicing entry on a self-initiated second pass, contacting maintenance and resolving it before acceptance. Completing the first pass only once the refuelling crew has cleared the aircraft, rather than while they are still present, would remove the need for the second pass. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable forms discipline.
texts_above.3: SP cross-checked the open write-ups and the servicing entries against the profile and the fuel plan for the sortie, clarifying one ambiguous entry with maintenance and annotating it before the walk-around began. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good forms review technique.
texts_above.4: SP reviewed the open write-ups and servicing entries against the profile and fuel plan with one ambiguous entry clarified and annotated before the walk-around began, leaving no question over the aircraft at any point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior forms review discipline.

error_modes.label: SEATING POSITION AND STRAP IN GEOMETRY
error_modes.source: technique:3.3 SEATING POSITION IN THE A/C

texts.0: SP, due to a seat height set by feel and not against the standard reference, sat with the upper part of the EADI display hidden behind the glare shield and with less than one fist separation between the top of the helmet and the canopy. The rudder pedals were left as found, so full travel of the rudder and brakes was not available, and the leg restraint lines were left with excessive slack. IP had to stop the strap in and reset seat, pedals and restraint lines before the canopy could be closed.
texts.1: SP, due to a sitting position that was not the same as on previous flights, set the seat so that the upper part of the EADI display was only just clear of the glare shield and did not check helmet to canopy clearance. Pedal adjustment and leg restraint slack were corrected only after IP asked for each check in turn. The cockpit was set to the lower limit of the standard through verbal prompting alone.
texts.2: SP, due to adjusting the rudder pedals before the seat and then losing the reference, initially set a position that did not allow full travel of the rudder and brakes. SP identified the restriction while checking full deflection during strap in, reset the pedals and took up the slack in the leg restraint lines without IP intervention. The final position gave the required EADI reference and canopy clearance.
texts.3: SP set the same sitting position as on every flight, with the upper part of the EADI display visible just below the glare shield and at least one fist separation between the top of the helmet and the canopy. The rudder pedals were adjusted to allow full travel of the rudder and brakes, and the leg restraint lines were left with enough length and minimal slack for full rudder deflection. No adjustment was required after strap in.
texts.4: SP set an exceptional cockpit position, establishing the EADI reference just below the glare shield, confirming the clearance required for the canopy breaker and checking full rudder and brake travel on both pedals before the straps were tightened. The leg restraint lines were routed with minimal slack and rechecked at full deflection, so nothing had to be adjusted again after strap in. Departures from the standard position were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP set a sitting position within standards, but helmet to canopy separation was at the minimum and the pedals gave full travel only with the ankle fully extended. The trend is toward a position that meets the reference on the ground while leaving no margin for the equipment actually worn in flight. SP is expected to standardize the seat and pedal settings and confirm them by full deflection on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP set the sitting position to the level expected at this stage, with the EADI reference and canopy clearance both achieved, due to the rudder pedals being adjusted before the seat and then reset once the reference was lost, requiring the check to be repeated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the seat first and the pedals second so the sequence is not repeated.
texts_at.2: SP reset the pedals and took up the leg restraint slack to give the required EADI reference and canopy clearance, due to the pedals being adjusted before the seat and losing the intended reference until it was reset during strap-in. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the EADI reference before adjusting the pedals, not after.
texts_at.3: SP set the seat with the EADI reference visible below the glare shield and confirmed full rudder and brake travel on both pedals, due to the leg restraint lines being taken up a step later in the strap-in than the reference check itself, though before the canopy was closed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to take up the restraint slack at the same point as the reference check rather than after it.

texts_above.2: SP identified a restriction on full rudder and brake travel during strap-in and reset the pedals and leg restraint lines to give the required EADI reference and canopy clearance without any assistance. Setting the seat before the pedals as a fixed order, rather than recovering from the reverse sequence, would remove the restriction before it appears. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured cockpit set-up.
texts_above.3: SP established the EADI reference just below the glare shield, confirmed canopy breaker clearance and checked full rudder and brake travel on both pedals before the straps were tightened, so nothing needed adjustment afterward. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise cockpit set-up.
texts_above.4: SP established the EADI reference, canopy clearance and full pedal travel in one sequence before the straps were tightened, with nothing requiring adjustment for the remainder of the strap-in. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate cockpit set-up.

error_modes.label: ENGINE START PARAMETER MONITORING AND OUTSIDE SCAN

texts.0: SP, due to closing the canopy without confirming that the canopy fracture system pin storage box over the left shoulder of the rear cockpit was closed, started the engine with the box open and then remained head down inside throughout the start. Interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed and the start ready light were not monitored as a set and no glance outside was made for possible aircraft movement or crew chief signals. IP had to call the start parameters and stop the sequence before it was complete.
texts.1: SP, due to a start scan built around the start ready light alone, watched the light but did not track interstage turbine temperature and gas generator speed through the acceleration. SP looked outside for the crew chief only when IP called for it. The start stayed at the lower limit of the standard and every outside check was made on IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held inside by the temperature indication, initially stopped glancing outside during the acceleration and missed the first crew chief signal. SP recognized the fixation, restored the scan between interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed, the start ready light and the ramp, and answered the signal before the crew chief repeated it. The start was completed to standard without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP confirmed the canopy fracture system pin storage box was closed before closing the canopy, then closely monitored interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed and the start ready light throughout the start. SP glanced outside occasionally to detect possible aircraft movement and crew chief signals, and informed the crew chief before activating any system that could endanger ground personnel. The start required no intervention.
texts.4: SP executed an exceptional start, checking the pin storage box and the propeller area first and then holding a scan that covered interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed and the start ready light while still catching each crew chief signal as it was given. Every system that could endanger ground personnel was called to the crew chief and operated only after the signal was repeated. Deviations from the prescribed sequence were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the start parameters within standards, but the outside glances were confined to the pauses in the sequence and the crew chief was watched rather than actively cleared. The trend is toward a start scan that reads the engine indications correctly while treating the ramp as somebody else's responsibility. SP is expected to clear the propeller area deliberately and read each crew chief signal between engine parameter checks on the next start.

texts_at.1: SP monitored the engine start to the level expected at this stage, tracking the start parameters and the ramp together, due to attention held inside by the temperature indication that briefly stopped the outside glance and let the first crew chief signal go unanswered until it was repeated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to alternate the scan between the parameters and the ramp on a fixed rhythm rather than staying inside until an indication settles.
texts_at.2: SP restored the scan between interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed, the start ready light and the ramp and answered the crew chief signal before it was repeated, due to attention held inside by the temperature indication that had briefly stopped the outside glance. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set a fixed interval for the outside glance so it does not depend on the temperature indication settling first.
texts_at.3: SP held a scan covering interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed, the start ready light and the ramp throughout the start, due to one crew chief signal answered a beat after it was given rather than as it appeared. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the ramp in peripheral view continuously rather than returning to it only at scan intervals.

texts_above.2: SP held a scan covering interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed, the start ready light and the ramp, recognizing and correcting one attention fixation on the temperature indication that had briefly stopped the outside glance before the crew chief signal was repeated. Holding the ramp in peripheral view continuously, rather than recovering it after a fixation, would remove the interruption from the scan. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent start-parameter monitoring.
texts_above.3: SP held a scan covering interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed and the start ready light while still catching every crew chief signal as it was given, calling each system that could endanger ground personnel and operating it only after the signal was repeated. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined start monitoring.
texts_above.4: SP read interstage turbine temperature, gas generator speed and the start ready light while catching every crew chief signal as it was given, with every system that could endanger ground personnel called and operated only after the signal was repeated. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless start monitoring.

error_modes.label: OBOGS CHECK SEQUENCE AND MASK SEAL VERIFICATION

texts.0: SP, due to donning the mask without checking the oxygen connections from the supply to the mask, did not establish system integrity and then omitted both the anti suffocation valve check and the mask seal check. The supply and concentration levers were never verified and no verbal challenge was passed to the other crewmember. IP had to stop the checklist and run the whole oxygen check again before taxi.
texts.1: SP, due to an oxygen check executed from memory rather than from the checklist, checked the connections and the levers but did not select EMERGENCY to check the mask seal and did not look for the no flow indication. The regulator indication was checked only when IP called for it, and the verbal challenge was passed only on prompting. The check finished at the lower limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to breathing through the check before the mask was seated, initially read a flow indication that did not settle and moved on toward the next item. SP recognized the incomplete seal, reseated the mask, selected EMERGENCY, momentarily held the breath and confirmed the black no flow indication before challenging the other crewmember. The check was completed to standard without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP checked the oxygen connections to ensure system integrity from the supply to the mask, donned the mask and checked the anti suffocation valve by breathing against the expected resistance. SP verified the supply lever on and the concentration lever normal, checked the mask seal by selecting EMERGENCY and momentarily holding the breath, and confirmed the no flow black indication on the regulator. SP then verbally challenged the other crewmember with the standard call.
texts.4: SP executed an exceptional oxygen check, tracing every connection from the supply to the mask before donning it and confirming the anti suffocation valve, the lever positions and the seal in one uninterrupted sequence. The no flow black indication was held long enough to be unambiguous and the verbal challenge to the other crewmember was passed and answered without delay. Departures from the prescribed check were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP completed the oxygen check within standards, but the seal check was cut short and the no flow indication was read while the mask was still being adjusted. The trend is toward a check that produces the correct words without producing certainty about the seal. SP is expected to hold the EMERGENCY selection until the black indication is stable before passing the verbal challenge on the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP completed the oxygen check to the level expected at this stage, verifying connections, levers and the mask seal, due to the regulator indication being checked only as a self-review step rather than as the immediate response to the EMERGENCY selection, delaying the verbal challenge slightly. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read the regulator indication as the immediate next step after selecting EMERGENCY.
texts_at.2: SP reseated the mask, selected EMERGENCY and confirmed the black no-flow indication before challenging the other crewmember, due to breathing through the check before the mask was fully seated, which produced an indication that did not settle before it was noticed and corrected. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the mask seal by feel before starting the breathing portion of the check.
texts_at.3: SP checked the oxygen connections, the anti-suffocation valve, the lever positions and the mask seal and confirmed the no-flow black indication, due to the verbal challenge to the other crewmember following a beat after the indication was confirmed rather than immediately with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to pass the challenge in the same motion as confirming the indication.

texts_above.2: SP checked the oxygen connections, the lever positions and the mask seal and confirmed the no-flow black indication, recognizing and reseating an incompletely sealed mask before the seal check was called complete. Confirming the seal by feel before starting the breathing portion, rather than reseating after an unsettled indication, would remove the correction from the check. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good oxygen check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP traced every connection from the supply to the mask before donning it and confirmed the anti-suffocation valve, the lever positions and the seal in one uninterrupted sequence, holding the no-flow indication long enough to be unambiguous. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good oxygen check technique.
texts_above.4: SP traced every oxygen connection, confirmed the anti-suffocation valve and lever positions and held the no-flow indication unambiguously in one uninterrupted sequence, with the verbal challenge passed and answered without delay. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent oxygen check discipline.

error_modes.label: NOSE WHEEL STEERING AND BRAKE APPLICATION TECHNIQUE DURING TAXI

texts.0: SP, due to carrying power well above idle once the aircraft was rolling, controlled taxi speed by riding the brakes and turned with differential braking while nose wheel steering remained engaged. Power was not reduced for the turns and the brakes were applied in abrupt, uneven steps. IP had to take the controls, stop the aircraft and reset the taxi power and braking technique.
texts.1: SP, due to a taxi executed with the power lever left forward of idle, needed continuous brake pressure to hold speed and applied differential braking on two turns with nose wheel steering engaged. Power was retarded to idle for the turns only after IP called for it each time. Taxi held at the lower limit of the standard and the technique was corrected entirely by verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to leaving the power up after the initial roll, initially rode the brakes along the first taxiway segment and made the first turn without retarding the power lever. SP recognized the excess power, returned the lever to idle, released the brakes and thereafter applied rudder and power reduction simultaneously for each turn, deselecting steering and using the inside brake for the one sharper turn. The remainder of the taxi was executed to standard without intervention.
texts.3: SP used idle power to initiate taxi and left the power lever at idle once the aircraft was rolling, applying the brakes smoothly, evenly and cautiously to control speed without riding them. For each nose wheel steering turn SP applied rudder in the desired direction and simultaneously reduced power to idle, and where a sharper turn was required deselected steering and used the inside brake. No differential braking was applied with steering engaged.
texts.4: SP handled power and brakes with exceptional precision, initiating the roll with a brief application of extra power and then holding idle, so brake use was reduced to occasional smooth applications. Every steering turn was made with rudder and simultaneous power reduction, the one sharper turn was made with steering deselected on the inside brake, and the aircraft was never allowed to accelerate between turns. Deviations from the prescribed technique were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP controlled the taxi within standards, but the power lever was returned to idle slightly late after each turn and the brakes were used in short repeated applications to absorb the surplus. The trend is toward speed control by brake rather than by power, with the wear on nose wheel steering and tire that follows. SP is expected to reduce power as the rudder goes in and let the aircraft decelerate before touching the brakes on the next taxi.

texts_at.1: SP taxied to the level expected at this stage, reducing power to idle for turns and applying rudder with steering engaged, due to the power lever being returned to idle a beat after the turn began rather than simultaneously with the rudder input, on most turns of the taxi. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move the power lever and the rudder together for every turn rather than in sequence.
texts_at.2: SP applied rudder and power reduction simultaneously for turns after the first taxiway segment, due to the power lever being left up through the initial roll and the first turn, corrected once the excess speed was recognized. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring the power lever to idle as the roll begins rather than after the first turn shows the excess.
texts_at.3: SP applied rudder and simultaneous power reduction to idle for each steering turn, using the inside brake for the one sharper turn with steering deselected, due to the power lever being returned to idle a fraction after each turn rather than exactly with it, though without any differential braking resulting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to bring rudder and power reduction together to the same instant on every turn.

texts_above.2: SP returned the power lever to idle and applied smooth, even braking after recognizing an excess taxi speed carried from the initial roll, then applied rudder and power reduction simultaneously for the remaining turns with no differential braking. Bringing the power lever to idle at the roll itself, rather than after the first turn shows the excess, would remove the initial correction from the taxi. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound taxi power and brake technique.
texts_above.3: SP initiated the roll with a brief application of extra power and then held idle, applying rudder and simultaneous power reduction for every steering turn and using the inside brake with steering deselected for the one sharper turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed taxi handling.
texts_above.4: SP held idle power for the whole taxi apart from a brief initial application, applying rudder with simultaneous power reduction for every turn and never allowing the aircraft to accelerate between them. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional taxi power and brake technique.

error_modes.label: OVER SPEED GOVERNOR CHECK EXECUTION AND CLEARING

texts.0: SP, due to starting the run up without ensuring the area immediately in front of and behind the aircraft was clear, advanced power abruptly and well above what was required to verify proper function of the overspeed governor. The control stick was left forward, the nose gear strut compressed and the aircraft crept forward while SP looked inside at the indications. IP had to retard the power, stop the aircraft and repeat the check.
texts.1: SP, due to a run up begun with attention entirely inside the cockpit, did not clear outside the aircraft during the check and advanced power faster than required. SP reduced power only after IP called the movement, and the brakes were pumped up and the check reattempted on IP direction. The check reached the lower limit of the standard through prompting alone.
texts.2: SP, due to relaxing the aft stick pressure as the power came up, allowed the nose gear strut to begin compressing early in the check.
